results.title: Transcript: Bill McNabb, Vanguard former Chairman and CEO
results.author: Barry Ritholtz
results.content:
The transcript from this week’s, MiB: Bill McNabb, Vanguard former Chairman and CEO, is below.
You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube (audio), and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here.
~~~
Masters in Business Bill McNabb, former Chairman and CEO, The Vanguard Group
Host: Barry Ritholtz  |  Bloomberg Radio
(00:00:02) Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news. This is Masters in Business with Barry Ritholtz on Bloomberg Radio.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:00:16): This week on the podcast, another extra, extra special guest. Bill McNabb was CEO and chairman at the Vanguard Group. He had been with the firm for 30 years, helping to take them up to trillions of dollars. We’ve spoken to him a couple of times in the past.
He discusses his post-Vanguard career, the boards he’s sitting on, all the fintech startups and venture capital he’s working with. I thought this conversation was fascinating, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my sit-down with William McNabb. Bill McNabb, welcome back to Bloomberg.
BILL McNABB (00:00:55): Oh, thanks, Barry. It’s great to be here.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:00:57): So the last two times you were here, you were running Vanguard Group. I’m curious, how does a guy who rowed at Dartmouth, taught Latin and coached at the Haverford School end up running the world’s largest mutual fund company?
BILL McNABB (00:01:16): So there’s an old saying that it’s better to be lucky than smart.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:01:21): My mom used to say that to me all the time.
BILL McNABB (00:01:23): And that really did apply. I got very lucky, Barry, in terms of just opportunities that happened to come my way. And I had incredible mentors who sort of helped take those opportunities and make more of them than maybe they would’ve been otherwise. And one thing led to another.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:01:43): Huh. Really interesting. So teaching Latin and coaching, what does that teach somebody like you about leadership that you were able to apply across three decades at Vanguard?
BILL McNABB (00:01:56): Yeah, I think there were two big things, and I was very fortunate to work for somebody at Vanguard who really lived this, and I’ll come back to that in a second. But the power of “we” versus “I.” I was coaching a rowing team, and no matter how good the individual athletes were, if they didn’t really exist in order to make the boat go faster, you weren’t going to win. And we had to really get that across to people, and that collective drive for success actually is incredibly applicable in the business world. I think the other thing, maybe a little more subtle, is you lead by example. Some of the people who talk about it, they theorize, and all these fancy sayings.
I’d rather just watch somebody do what they do really well. And if they’re building good teams, just that example of how they do it is really worth emulating. I worked for Jack Brennan, as you know, and I think you’ve had Jack on here before as well. And Jack really lived that. For me, when I got to Vanguard, the “we” versus “I” was very apparent in how he was driving the firm, and no one led by example better than Jack.
And when you’ve grown up in that world as a coach and an athlete, and then you get it reinforced professionally early in your career, it becomes a way of thinking.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:03:24): Yeah. Big fan of Jack Brennan. Loved what he did. When you joined Vanguard in ’86, it was obviously a fraction of where it is today.
It was far less than a trillion dollars. And even in the mid-eighties, I mean, that was the beginning of the bull market that started in ’82. You had Peter Lynch and the Fidelity Magellan Fund. Berkshire Hathaway was on the rise, stock picking was on the rise.
I guess I could say indexing was a fringe idea. What did the firm look like back in the mid-eighties? Did you have any idea what was coming your way over the next couple of decades?
BILL McNABB (00:04:05): This is why I said it’s really better to be lucky than smart. I did not see this incredible explosion coming. What attracted me to Vanguard was I was working here in New York for what’s now JPMorgan Chase, and was getting a little frustrated with a lot of things and decided it was probably time to go. And again, one of my mentors said to me, go find a place where the values match your own.
And when I went in and interviewed with Jack Brennan and then Jack Bogle, I found, it was like, wow, this is so different. And there was tremendous appeal. And so I did it really based on gut and intuition at the time. And so when I interviewed with Jack Bogle, the funny story was, he had data pulled out, a bunch of stuff, and he’s like, we just crossed $15 billion under management and I have no idea how we’re going to get to 20.
So I don’t know why you would come here. You’re doing big things on Wall Street. And I didn’t even really have a response. And then he went on, he goes, but of course, and for the next hour and a half, I got a lecture about everything that needed to change in the asset management business.
I go home and my wife says to me, how’d it go? I said, I don’t know. I didn’t say anything. But she goes, well, what are you going to do?
And I said, well, if he offers me the job, I’m going. Because there was just something there, the passion and the drive and the really contrarian view. So the early days, look, we paid as much attention to active management as Fidelity did. So Fidelity had Peter Lynch in the Magellan Fund.
We had John Neff in the Windsor Fund. Arguably one of the two or three greatest value investors in history. And Jack himself was very much making sure that we were competitive.
Money market funds were just taking off. And we got into the money market fund wars. It’s hard for people to imagine today, but yields were 17, 18% at different times.
And Dreyfus, Fidelity and Vanguard were the three money market fund giants. We each had a couple billion dollars, but everybody was comparing yields. And so active management and the yield on the money market fund in the early days, those were like the big drivers.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:06:22): So my pet thesis, to put this into context: $15 billion in the early eighties, just about $15 trillion today. That’s just a crazy thousand-fold increase. That’s just an insane run. My theory is the late nineties, the scandals, the crashes, the analyst scandal, the accounting scandal, the IPO scandal, all one after another.
I think a lot of people just threw their hands up and said, you know what, just buy me the whole market. Let me know when I have enough to retire. Is that oversimplifying what happened?
Or is that a real factor?
BILL McNABB (00:07:00): So I would say that’s the psychological part of it. There was also the math part of it, which is on an after-tax basis, index funds beat 90% of active equities over any rolling ten-year period.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (00:07:15): Anything more than a decade.
BILL McNABB (00:07:16): Anything more than a decade. So if you were a long-term investor and you wanted to win, you indexed. BARRY RITHOLTZ (01:18:36): Right. There’s a long history there, which we will discuss offline. But when Brennan said to me, hey, I’ve been a reader of your stuff, when I first met him at some large conference room lunch 20 years ago, my head exploded.
BILL McNABB (01:18:56): I might’ve been one of the people who pushed it that way. But to me it was a really important thing. And I think, like today, people aren’t talking about leverage that much. And I worry about leverage. When you look at what the hyperscalers are doing in terms of the bond market right now, and a couple of them are not net cash flow positive because of all the infrastructure that they’re building, the leverage in the system. Private credit had its moment a year ago or whatever, six months ago, and that was one you could see coming.
I worry a lot about leverage. No one’s talking about it. When I first started out, that way of thinking, that contrarianness, was not part of how I had been trained or brought up. But again, this is where Jack Bogle, Jack Brennan, John Neff, the great value investor, they were really impactful.
BARRY RITHOLTZ (01:20:01): I was going through an old piece I was writing and never finished, and I found some notes, and I can’t figure out whose line this is. It feels like I’m stealing it from somebody. Equity crises bruise, debt crises maim. And I’ve been unable to track that down, and it doesn’t sound like something I would’ve written.
But anytime I use something from someone, I’m usually very, very fastidious about making sure the quote is attributed correctly. But it just reminds us that leverage kills. Look at what’s going on in Korea with their three x and five x funds as those unwind. Man, they’ve had a great run, and they’ve given a ton of it back.
Because of the leverage. Bill, I could talk to you for two more hours.
Thank you for being so generous with your time. This has been utterly fascinating. We have been speaking with Bill McNabb, former chairman and CEO of the Vanguard Group, board member at IBM and UnitedHealth, senior advisor to Venrock, as well as board member and advisor to so many startups. If you enjoy this conversation, well, check out any of the 654 we’ve done over the past 12 years.
You can find those at Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Bloomberg, wherever you get your favorite podcasts from. I would be remiss if I didn’t thank the crack team that helps put these conversations together each week. My audio engineer is Alexis Noriega. Anna Luke is my producer. Sean Russo is my researcher.
I’m Barry Ritholtz. You’ve been listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio.
~~~
results.summary:
Former Vanguard CEO Bill McNabb discusses his transition from leading the world’s largest mutual fund company to his current roles in corporate governance and the venture capital startup ecosystem.

### Key Points
- Bill McNabb served as CEO and Chairman of The Vanguard Group, overseeing its growth to over $5 trillion in assets during his tenure.
- He currently serves on the boards of IBM and UnitedHealth Group, focusing on talent, strategy, and corporate culture.
- McNabb acts as a senior advisor to the venture capital firm Venrock, where he mentors founders of fintech startups like Altruist, Vanilla, and Finny.
- He emphasizes the importance of long-term investment discipline and warns against the risks of excessive leverage in modern financial markets.
- McNabb advocates for a "human-in-the-loop" approach to financial advice, arguing that technology should enable advisors rather than replace them.

### Why it Matters
McNabb’s shift from a massive, passive-investing mutual fund giant to the agile world of venture-backed fintech highlights a broader industry trend toward hyper-personalized, tech-enabled wealth management. His insights into governance and succession planning provide a roadmap for how legacy corporations and new startups can navigate market volatility while maintaining a focus on long-term investor outcomes.

results.title: iPhone 18 Pro Event Could Hit Apple Shares, KeyBanc Warns
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
Apple's September 9 iPhone announcement event could become a negative catalyst for the stock, KeyBanc Capital Markets warns.
In a research note seen by Investing.com, KeyBanc said the event could motivate investors to weigh pricing decisions against the impact of higher costs on demand and margins. KeyBanc added that Apple faces a choice to either raise prices broadly to offset gross margin pressure, which could hurt unit volumes and trigger "sticker shock," or raise prices more selectively.
This could invite greater scrutiny of margins and raise the prospect of further price increases later down the line. The firm maintained an "Underweight" rating on Apple and a $250 price target, against a share price of $324.96 at the time of publication.
KeyBanc models total iPhone 18 lineup builds at around 80 million units across the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 and first quarter of fiscal 2027, down from roughly 91 million units a year earlier. The firm attributed most of the decline to the absence of a base iPhone 18 model in this part of the product cycle, with higher pricing and a richer product mix expected to partially offset the lower volumes.
KeyBanc is also expecting a $150 price increase for the iPhone 18 Pro, raising it to $1,249, and a $200 increase for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, raising it to $1,399. The firm expects the foldable "iPhone Ultra" to start at $2,199.
KeyBanc also pointed to a historical pattern of Apple shares weakening around iPhone announcements, with the stock averaging a 0.72% decline on announcement day over the past five years and a 1.22% decline five trading days later. Apple's "Surprise and shine" event commences at 10 a.m. Pacific time on Wednesday, September 9.

results.title: Solaris in Xenogears Is A Disturbing But Fascinating Journey Into Human Nature
results.author: Peter Tieryas
results.content:
Xenogears might not be the best JRPG on the PS1 due to its format shift in the second half, but it has one of the most thought-provoking stories on the system. The first half still remains one of the most ambitious and complex narratives ever told. I still discover new things with each playthrough and feel I’d have to write a whole book just to describe all of my thoughts on it. Instead, I’ll focus on the sky kingdom of Solaris which comes just before the end of Disc 1 and epitomizes what makes the game so revered among those who’ve had the chance to experience it.
Stars of Tears
Plotwise, there’s a lot going on in Xenogears. In the opening anime, the colony ship called the Eldridge crashes into a planet with the cryptic text, “You shall be as gods” repeating on the screen. Thousands of years later, Kislev and Aveh are at war. The main protagonist, Fei, tries to figure out what all the flashbacks he gets mean while juggling his fractured self that somehow connects with his ability to unleash massive power on his gear. The floating city of Shevat holds many secrets that tie in with the conflict and it’s all somehow connected with a war 500 years ago and the 12 Anima Relics of God. Ethos (a religious group) and Gebler (a secret military faction) are both pulling the strings and causing the land-dwellers or “lambs” to fight each other. Meanwhile some masked stranger named Grahf wants to awaken Fei so they can kill god. There’s so many characters in Xenogears with clashing agendas that whenever I think I’m starting to understand what’s going on, a new twist or character upends everything. It feels like a science fiction-philosophy-psychology-religious buffet with the devs mixing and matching in ways that kept me constantly intrigued.
Director and co-writer, Tetsuya Takahashi paid tribute to many of his favorite works in the game. The Sacred Empire of Solaris is named after the SF classic Soviet film and book that’s about an oceanic planet called Solaris. The planet turns out to be conscious and can physically manifest people’s deepest secrets, kind of like a Silent Hill in space. In Xenogears, Fei learns that Solaris is secretly funding and directing the Ethos and Gebler to exacerbate tensions and keep the lambs in perpetual strife. The party has to make their way up to the kingdom by destroying the Three Surface Gates that hide its existence from the rest of the world.
On initially landing in Solaris, the team is physically inverted, walking upside down on the floating city. I took it as foreshadowing that everything they thought they knew was going to be turned upside down, and it is. Fei is split from the group and ends up arriving at 3rd Class F Block, which is the lowest section of the city.
As soon as he emerges from his cell, he hears someone yell, “Something’s wrong with all of you! Working like machines day after day. You have no will! This isn’t living!!’ They’re seized by a security cube, flown over to a giant pit, then dropped down without a warning to their death. No one tries to protest or object to his treatment. Instead, one of the citizens complains, “It’s malcontents like him that get us all punished. It kills me to think that all our work to raise our block’s rank is ruined.”
The citizens are split into three separate classes and those in the Honeycomb are in the 3rd, and lowest, class. They focus on staying compliant and alive. Fei meets up with one of his team members, Elly, who reveals that 3rd class citizens are called “Worker Bees,” and provide “manual labor vital to the support of Solaris’ core.” They’re treated as disposable.
In another cell, someone is worried they’ll be “rearranged” and, having no other source of comfort, begs God for support. But his prayers go unanswered. As soon as you leave, the honey comb is removed and “rearranged” as they feared. You later learn that the process involves a mix of “brainwashing and amnesia,” often targeting those who try to escape. Language is just as critical a tool of repression as those Security Cubes. Note that they’re not being “punished” or “imprisoned,” at least in terms of the political/legal lexicon, but “rearranged,” almost like it was a matter of housekeeping or sanitation.
The distinction by class also creates another form of institutionalized control in promising those in 3rd Class a chance to move up the ranks. A 3rd class Solaris citizen can also regard themselves as more valuable than the Surface Dwellers which, as mentioned, they disparagingly call “lambs.”
You eventually meet a man from the surface named Samson who Fei mistakes for a close friend that was killed, Timothy. Timothy’s senseless murder in the early hours of the game was what triggered a mental collapse in Fei and it would appear he’s still haunted by his death. Samson gives Fei a work permit to help him escape to the upper level. But during an ID scan, Timothy gets vaporized. Solaris is merciless.
But why? There are thematic parallels between the sky city and Tiphares from Battle Angel Alita (though I don’t think it’s ever been explicitly stated that Tiphares was an inspiration). In both, the surface is hellish and rife with conflict. In both, this elevated city should be a utopia, especially with all its technological advancements. But despite the abundance, the stratification between the 3rd Class and 1st Class is a wide chasm, bridged by the commercialism of the 2nd class area.
With Elly’s ID, you’re able to enter the 2nd Class district. It’s no coincidence that the classes are segmented by height while security zones prevent intermingling. You physically have to ascend to get to the upper levels. The architecture is being used by the system as a further technique of reinforcing power and control. Arbot Plaza and its surrounding areas in Etrenank are full of shopping stores and holographic advertisements.
But social customs are also under the supervision of the government. Central Control Bureau arrange marriages for their citizens, proudly stating their motto: “Good matches make good descendants.” Another citizen declares, “There are none of the crimes, disasters or wars like on earth. Science makes everything possible for us.”
Fei learns that saving a game file is sending data to the Control Bureau. A girl plays with her Alloy Imperial Gear toy while yelling, “Purge the Lambs.” A citizen casually notes, “There seems to be a big struggle on the surface. But it has absolutely nothing to do with us.” You find a couple in an apartment having dance practice with their holographic teacher. Someone is even a fan of Tifa from Final Fantasy 7. It’s a paradise in comparison, until you notice the Security Cubes patrolling the sidewalks and the unspoken threat their presence makes clear.
Fei has to make his way to the plaza to watch the Dedication celebration. Your destruction of the gates has threatened the illusion of stability and the Emperor has to calm the masses with a political rally. There’s a smug arrogance to Empires, a disdainful attitude that bread and circuses and a let them eat cake indifference can suppress any discontent.
It’s also backed by religious discourse. Solaris, which is all too familiar with using both military force (in Gebler) and religious orthodoxy (in Ethos) for the purposes of maintaining authority has perfected the ceremonial aesthetics of bullshitting. But the fact that they felt the need to address it also betrays their concern.
The Emperor refers to the crowd as his “children.” Combined with the earlier message about prearranged marriages, it’s clear they’re trying to replace the family unit with one directed by the government. The emperor lies to the crowd that the destruction of the gates was planned and that the time for their impending immortality has come. He also reveals that they’ve opened the door to Mahanon, “the place where god rests, the source of wisdom and power…. Let’s show stupid beasts, the Lambs our real power.” With ships positioned above, fireworks go off, the masses cheering as they get a magnificent show. A mix of jingoism, marginalization, and spectacle, this sequence gives us more insight into how Solaris has ruled over the world for so long.
Krelian, who’s named after the alien character Karellan from the novel Childhood’s End, shows up to give more assurance to the masses. His intentions are similar to the alien in the book in wanting to guide humanity to a new future, albeit a more sinister one. Elly reveals that Krelian is the real leader of Solaris. His appearance triggers a flashback in Fei. It turns out they somehow knew each other, but it’s still not clear how or when that was, only that it was in the past. One funny thing I noticed is that Fei seems to have worn the exact same clothes back then too. He really likes his getup!
In the present, Krelian reveals that Fei’s friends have been taken captive and will be disposed of in the “Soylent System.” The arbitrariness of their punishment struck me. Does Solaris not have a judicial system? Then it occurred to me that in the opening sequence, the Security Cube just dropped the person without any semblance of a trial. Shortly after the ceremony, Fei ends up attracting the attention of security who then proceed to attack him and Elly. Again, no due process, or even the pretense of one. In many authoritarian structures, the need for order and justice is often used to legitimize repression. In Solaris, the execution of justice is left solely to the Security Cubes who make the determination as they see fit.
It’s not clear if there was any kind of human supervision either. When Elly and Fei escape to the 1st Class/Gazel Citizen level, no cubes follow, nor do any human soldiers arrive. Automated machines determine who lives, who gets rearranged, and who dies. But the citizens of Solaris never question the system or the programming logic behind it. Instead, they attack those who don’t comply with the rules, even if it’s subject to the interpretation of a machine.
Up in the 1st Class area, Elly invites Fei into her house. Their residence is massive, contrasting with the tiny cells of the Worker Bees and even the bigger apartments of the 2nd Class Citizens. Her mom greets them, but Elly doesn’t want to answer too many questions and takes Fei into her room. He’s in awe as he states, “It must be bigger than the village chief’s!” And in a moment of bathroom sociopolitics, he’s also amazed she has one in her room.
Elly takes a shower and reveals that her parents aren’t really her parents. Most likely, her nanny, a land dweller, was her real mom. Fei also takes a shower and is amazed how good it feels. After they both clean up, they go to her dad’s room and break into his computer. The password is her name backwards. It’s a subtle point, but it shows her dad, Erich, cares for his daughter.
Elly finds out how to break into the palace and rescue their friends thanks to the information on his terminal. Erich, as a Solaris official and former superintendent of the Soylent System, has a lot of access. But then he arrives and doesn’t like seeing the land dweller accompanying his daughter. Family drama ensues and her dad calls security. The sequence ends with Fei voluntarily leaving Elly behind.
It is important to note that the guards who come are human, not the Security Cubes, and they give Erich a warning when he resists their attempt to take Elly away. Even law enforcement is meted out differently based on class. Also, Erich’s biggest fear is being cast down to the 3rd Class, not prison, showing how the hierarchical system coerces those even at the highest tiers.
As I descended with Fei down to the 3rd Class area and passed through the 2nd Class Area again, I was surprised that life was proceeding as normal. Even if I couldn’t understand the Solarians without Elly to translate, the Emperor’s performance had been sufficient for the citizens, most still focused on shopping or getting to work in their hover vehicles. At the same time, what options do they have? If they stand up against the madness, they’ll be excised. Better to act like a lamb and pretend like everything is great. At least that’s what every citizen tells themselves as they play their part in the normalization of repression.
Fei meets up with another of his team members, the doctor Citan, who’s been a steadfast companion throughout the game. They also reunite with Elly, who reveals that her parents were arrested. Krelian had ordered her incarceration, but her parents had resisted long enough for her to escape. Although she’s worried about them, she decides to focus on saving their friends with the plan of helping her parents later on.
Bonds of Sea and Fire
There are a lot of random battles in the next area. Fortunately, I really like the battle system in Xenogears. The combos and deathblows add an arcade element to turn-based combat. You have to chain attacks in a specific order to trigger the deadlier moves. Like many fans have noted, I love how Fei makes grunts during his attacks and yells, “Booyah!” as he executes his final blow. Citan’s martial arts are great (so cool how casually he does the splits) and Elly uses rods and magic in an elegantly smooth fashion. I also love how when the deathblows activate, time slows down as the characters gather energy. Their moves are so quick, they even leave behind an afterimage.
The battle system is similar when you’re fighting in the giant gears. It’s a great feeling when you face an enemy that you struggled with in human form, but can totally crush in the giant suits as they’re tiny in comparison. There are limitations placed by fuel. I don’t know if Neon Genesis Evangelion was an influence (it came out around the same time as Xenogears), but in both, I appreciated the realism that the fuel restrictions added to mecha combat. At the same time, I ran out more times than I’d have liked and it was frustrating. Even with the charger, there wasn’t any easy way to refuel during battle. Then again, this forced me to prepare better by buying better equipment and upgrades (git gud!).
Fei, Citan, and Elly make their way through the garbage dump in Solaris up to the Soylent System factory to find their friends. They find some containers with food. Fei and Elly, who are hungry, decide to gorge themselves. Citan refrains. The noise they make as they eat sounds like a bouncing ball and is kind of funny.
“I wonder what kind of meat this is,” Elly poses later (asked no Castlevania protagonist upon finding meat in the walls).
They learn shortly afterwards when they track the source of the conveyor belt and see the remains of bodies being pumped out. “The organism experiment and its disposal facility,” Citan announces. The food they just ate was people.
Bruh, couldn’t you have told them before they ate it? Then again, maybe he just wanted to hammer in the point. This is really fucked up.
Seeing the corpses spat out on a conveyor belt is revolting enough. But their endless number is just as appalling. The food isn’t just there to feed the surface dwellers either. Chemical ingredients are engineered specifically to keep their behavior supplicant and also to maintain their Limiters. On top of that, the experiments in the lab are how the wels you’ve been fighting are created. The food is actually a mix of humans and wels mashed together into canned mystery meat. “To end a person’s life and then consume their flesh,” Citan says. “Is that, permissible…?”
I appreciate a good tribute in any work. But I wish they could have used another name for the system as even general familiarity with the film telegraphs the secret. In the film, Soylent Green, the world’s problems are solved by the eponymous food that’s supposedly made out of plankton. The big reveal at the end of the film is that “Soylent Green is people!” (A side note on Soylent Green. The book that the film was based on, Make Room! Make Room! did not feature the macabre twist about humans. It was the film adaptation that added the cannibalistic reveal).
They exit the factory area by taking a lift almost like they’re emerging from the dregs. In addition to the security drones, the team has to fight the Neo Wels, which are the updated experimental subjects with pulsing veins. One of the most haunting fights is against Dorothy. She’s another subject that has been mutated into a monster. Strangely, physical attacks heal her, while healing items wound her. It’s eerie as I wondered why her physical condition was flipped that way.
Eventually, they come across Solaris’ massive Omnigear. In the adjacent room, there are a bunch of captives being turned into Wels. But they’re not being shown beautiful films and played comforting music like at the clinics of Soylent Green. They’re caged, their humanity slipping away. One of them warns you not to release him as he knows he’s mutating.
This whole section is long and easy to get lost in. But it’s also a mentally harrowing excavation of the human cost that keeps Solaris going. It’s designed to be stressful. Once they reach the end of the factory, Citan explains this facility was where humans were created 10,000 years ago. The Emperor and the Ministry were the first of the humans. But the governing ministry were killed during the Diabolos Invasion and only existed as “data in memory banks.”
The Soylent Facility was supposed to help them resurrect themselves and keep the Emperor alive, but was turned into an all-purpose enslavement center. Save spots send data to the Gazel Ministry which they can exploit. “They’re transferring and taking living data via Memory Cubes to the Ministry so they can use them to resurrect their bodies?!” Elly asks in shock. Citan confirms it. I couldn’t help but think of parallels to social media and how our uploaded data is being used.
Elly is suspicious and demands to know how Citan knows all of this as even officers at her level have no idea. As she presses her interrogation, the lights go out. Fei makes his way through the darkness, only to find himself restrained by a force ring that has cut his nerve signals. Members of the Gazel Ministry appear as digital data on big screens and confront Fei.
“You already own the world!” Fei yells at them. “What more do you want?” It’s a good question, but the answer is not what I was expecting.
The Gazel members reveal they’re aliens, connecting them to the ship that crashed in the opening anime. They want to resurrect God, raise the ark, and return to the stars to rule over the universe. Solaris is insignificant to them, just a means to an end. They also plan on using the bodies of Bart and the other party members as vessels they can inhabit. Helping them to achieve this was their “Guardian Angel” Citan (Guardian Angel could be a reference to the short story of the same name that Childhood’s End was based on). Turns out your friend is a traitor who’s been watching you this entire time under the orders of the emperor. Or so it seems. In another twist, Citan has his own agenda that doesn’t align with the ministry. So does Krelian, who they’re counting on to help them physically resurrect themselves. Krelian checks Elly and discovers the “Urobolos Ring” in the introns of her genetic code, a reference to the Ouroboros, the giant snake that eats itself and represents the eternal cycle of life.
Xenogears is a narrative roller coaster ride. I’ll admit, even after I replayed the game three times, I had to rewatch playthroughs just to make sense of some of the plot points. This isn’t like modern day games that inundate you with glossaries and codices to explain everything in even more detail. What you experience is what you get. My love for the minutia and lore of the game is the reason I bought a memory card devoted specifically to backup saves after key points in the game.
The whole next section accelerates with even more plot twists. Ramsus, Elly’s old commander, is having a breakdown over his inability to defeat Fei. Citan reveals he’s actually working with you and double crosses the ministry. Billy and Bart try to have their limiters removed, which are mostly psychological and designed to make them defer to the Ministry and the Emperor. But then Citan reveals Elly never had a limiter (which even the citizens of Solaris get).
Fei meets up with the rest of the crew. Elly also is happy to learn that her parents were rescued by one of the shopkeepers, Hammer. Now they have to fight their way out. But once they reach the exit, Hammer betrays them. Driven by his insecurities, he’s agreed to capture Elly and take her back to Krelian. Elly’s mom steps in the way in an attempt to protect her, but gets killed. Hammer, shocked by his own action, flees. But then Grahf shows up with the Executioner. Fei and company fight hard, but Grahf is about to overpower them. Then Elly’s dad arrives in a new gear, telling Elly to escape. The Executioner/Miang blows up her dad’s gear. Elly’s furious and ether starts to flow within her. Fei also is outraged and his gear wakes up without anyone to control it. You know shit is getting real when it changes to a FMV sequence as Weltall’s true form blasts off towards the sky city.
The Id, which represents the unconscious and unfiltered desires that drive humans, is unleashed in Fei. That form of Fei ends up destroying the entire city. Oops. Shouldn’t have pissed him off. Except it seems Krelian and Miang actually wanted this?
At this point, Citan explains a lot of the history of Fei, how his Id form worked for Grahf as an assassin, but their personalities are dissociated from each other. The Emperor thinks he’s Anonelbe, or a man of God. We also see the Gazel Ministry discussing future plans with Krelian. Even though we get much more insight into the situation, somehow, I was left with more questions than when I began.
The fall of Solaris marks the end of Disc 1. As those who’ve played the game know, Disc 2 changes to a visual novel format with occasional battles.
I actually liked the second disc a whole bunch, but I also knew that the change was coming. For those who didn’t, it must have been a shock. Square’s execs actually recommended the team end the game after the destruction of Solaris as they were out of time and budget. The format of the second disc was what Takahashi proposed so that he could finish the tale. I’m glad they did, but it would have made for one helluva cliffhanger if they’d gone with that original idea of ending the game here.
The Wounded Shall Advance Into the Light
I was happy to revisit Xenogears in 2026. While I’m admittedly making thematic connections on my own, I could totally see a future where the AIs of old leaders rule the world like the Ministry of Gazel without people even knowing. There’s CEOs even now who are digitally cloning themselves for the employees to interact with. The idea of “worker bees” living in terror and doing their best just to survive while a middle class thrives in indifference thanks to their commercial palliatives is also not hard to envision.
Ultimately, was it worth it for those in charge of Solaris? They wasted a whole lot of resources exploiting the population so they could get back to the stars instead of using their technology to help people. Ironically, if they’d worked together and treated them well, they probably would have had a better chance at success. All sides could have benefited and there would have been no need for all the subterfuge.
Instead, the Gazel’s belief in their own superiority led to treatment that provoked discontent, rebellion, and eventually their own annihilation. Through all the twists and turns, it comes down to power, or what they perceive to be that power. But raw Id, or human nature as symbolized by Fei’s other form, revolts against it, totally crushing their schemes. Whether it be destroying a god, or trying to become one, the struggle of egos is at the forefront of most of the game’s characters. It’s to the point where humans are devouring other humans just to survive, even though that sustenance is what keeps them leashed in the first place. In that sense, the gears with the anima are a deified physical form of humanity, unbound by the fragility of flesh. There are also religious parallels with the old ideas of Gnosticism and the Demiurge who traps people in a sleep that prevents them from recognizing their divine origins. That’s also apparent in the ministry’s attempt to “limit” Lambs and prevent them from escaping a mental and physical prison within their own bodies.
Fei’s portrayal, as a complex ziggurat of three personalities, resonates in the modern era. There’s the impulses of the unconscious, but also the social construct made by our relationships, and a final, craven “coward” traumatized by existence itself who somehow bridges the two and uses each persona as needed.
Xenogears juggles these philosophical and psychological quandaries in the same way. Fei is the “JRPG” on top of the ideas, the normal facade Takahashi wants to use to dissect the Id. Volume two is in a sense that story in its purest form. But there’s also the fear of exposing the ideas without that cover. Hence the bridge that crosses the gap. That mask is ripped away in Disc 2.
The thing I love about Xenogears is that that’s just my interpretation of events. Someone else will probably have something completely different. And that’s not just okay, but the point.
I thought a lot about the fall of Solaris, all the lives lost and how wasteful it was. If only the leaders had been more reasonable instead of pushing Fei to the breaking point. What if the people had stood up against the ministers who never cared about them to begin with? What should people do in a world where God’s existence is inextricably connected with their own destruction?
I don’t have the answers, but I recall what Citan says to Fei while he’s taken captive, an accusation that is both insightful and damning and ties in with the bigger themes of Xenogears. “It is much easier to be given a place to belong than to make one yourself. Under total surveillance, there is no need to bear the risk of maintaining one’s own individuality. They simply live under the delusion of being an ‘individual.’ What could be easier?”
results.summary:
The classic PlayStation JRPG *Xenogears* remains a landmark title for its ambitious, philosophically dense narrative that explores complex themes of identity, authoritarian control, and Gnostic religious symbolism.

### Key Points
- *Xenogears* features a multi-layered plot involving the floating city of Solaris, which maintains power through class stratification and the systematic repression of surface-dwelling "lambs."
- The game’s narrative incorporates heavy science fiction and psychological influences, including references to the film *Solaris*, *Battle Angel Alita*, and *Childhood’s End*.

I usually just do my evil laugh.

A merger lasts until one entity has extracted all the value it can from the other and then sells it for parts.
Why does your face look like that?
Thank you! I used generative AI and a 3D printer to create it.
What keeps you up at night?
That there are Hawaiian islands not yet under my personal control.

results.title: Do tech billionaires dream of shared abundance? We should probably just tax them
results.author: Carl Rhodes, Professor of Business and Society, University of Technology Sydney
results.content:
On July 24, Elon Musk was interviewed by The Economist’s editor Zanny Minton Beddoes. The 85-minute discussion ranged from Musk’s business ventures to the war in Ukraine, China’s technological power and the immense capabilities of artificial intelligence.
Pressed by Beddoes on how his companies will make money in the future, he boldly prophesied that “money won’t matter in 2036”. Musk proposed that within a decade, money for “food, housing, transport, entertainment” will be overabundant. That will be a time where “the robots and AI are providing more goods and services than any human could possibly consume”. And it will produce so much, scarcity will be virtually eliminated, resulting in “incredible abundance for all”.
This wasn’t a one-off prediction. Earlier this year, in a podcast interview, he suggested we not “worry about squirrelling money away for retirement”, because in ten or 20 years, “saving for a retirement will be irrelevant”.
Review: We Need to Tax Billionaires – Gabriel Zucman (Basic Books)
According to Musk, AI will lead us to a “post-scarcity society”. In his techno-utopian future, work will be optional. All will be well, Musk claims, so long as we have AI that “has good values, that cares about humanity and that wants us to be happy and prosper”.
Trust me, I’m a tech billionaire
Before we all rush out and empty our savings accounts, we might well ask what mechanisms will translate the abundance generated by technology into a society where, as Musk promises, “everyone can have a penthouse”.
Musk’s explanation was posted on X last April:
Universal HIGH INCOME via checks [cheques] issued by the Federal government is the best way to deal with unemployment caused by AI.
AI/robotics will produce goods & services far in excess of the increase in the money supply, so there will not be inflation.
Musk’s optimism is not unique among his fellow tech billionaires. While they disagree on many things, they share a common faith that technological abundance will somehow translate into social abundance.
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg’s recent missive The Future is for Everyone presents no less than “a philosophy for how we can best use superintelligence to ensure it improves all of our lives, work, communities, freedom and safety”.
In Zuckerberg’s estimation, if “superintelligence beyond human capacity” is available to everybody, the resulting gains in productivity and economic growth will ultimately benefit everyone.
Faith in technology is also summoned in venture capitalist Marc Andreessen’s Techno-Optimist Manifesto:
We believe there is no conflict between capitalist profits and a social welfare system that protects the vulnerable. In fact, they are aligned – the production of markets creates the economic wealth that pays for everything else we want as a society.
What is largely missing from these accounts is any serious proposition for the political and institutional mechanisms through which this abundance will be distributed.
The question is pertinent given Musk’s status as the richest person in history. His fortune illustrates the point, as it is not the result of scarcity, but control over assets and government support. Distribution is fundamentally a question of power, ownership and political institutions.
The question of distribution
It is precisely the question of distribution that Gabriel Zucman addresses in his book We Need to Tax Billionaires.
Zucman is not a tech billionaire. He is professor at the Paris School of Economics, a co-director of the World Inequality Lab, and one of the world’s most influential economists working on wealth and taxation.
His book wears its heart on its sleeve: we need to tax billionaires. The reason, according to Zucman, is simple. Wealth does not distribute itself. However impressive the productive capacities of AI might become, under the current political arrangements wealth will remain concentrated.
We Need to Tax Billionaires is not a dry treatise on the dismal science of taxation. In this short and highly readable book, Zucman offers a provocative account of how the ultra-rich use their power and influence, aided by armies of lawyers and accountants, to minimise their tax obligations and enhance their privileged position.
Zucman doesn’t just describe tax avoidance, he quantifies it. He shows that across Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States, it is consistently the case that, in his words, “those at the top of the wealth distribution chain pay virtually no income tax”.
What techniques do billionaires deploy to do this that the rest of us can’t access? The most prevalent way, according to Zucman, is to shelter income in personal holding companies, retaining profits in those companies rather than receiving them as income.
Meanwhile, their fortunes grow through unrealised and untaxed capital gains as the value of their assets rises. Wealth and power grows. Taxable income all but disappears.
Using France as an example, Zucman shows taxation is broadly progressive across the vast majority of the population. Working-class people pay an effective tax rate of around 45%, the middle classes around 50% and the upper classes slightly more.
At the very top, however, the pattern reverses. For the “ultra-rich”, the rate falls drastically to 13%. When it comes to income tax alone, the ultra-rich pay just 2%. What this all means is that billionaires are “skirting their responsibilities to make a fair contribution to society”.
As Zucman goes on to show, France exemplifies the more general case that “in every country for which data is available, income tax vanishes at the top of the pyramid”.
The implications are stark. As Zucman argues:
Global tax evasion has been one of the linchpins of rising inequality and government debt worldwide. It has also led many to lose hope in the very possibility of a fairer society, creating a breeding ground for the reactionary political movements that are thriving today.
There is nothing here of the shared abundance promised by the tech billionaires. Instead, Zucman shows how extreme wealth reproduces itself, and how those who possess it deploy considerable resources to take an unequal status quo and make it even less equal.
Zucman is not arguing the economy should be restructured so as to abolish the existence of billionaires. Neither is he suggesting absolute economic equality. France’s richest person, Bernard Arnault, may have accused Zucman of being a “far-left activist”, but he is not.
Zucman’s argument is more democratic than socialist. His point is straightforward. Democracy demands that citizens are treated equally under the law. The tax avoidance practices of the ultra-rich violate that principle.
Democracy needs a wealth tax
How billionaires retain and expand their wealth and power is only half the story. Zucman hits his stride when he outlines what needs to be done to get them to meet their democratic responsibilities and pay their fair share.
Income tax is not the answer, given billionaires’ earnings come in the form of corporate profits and assets rather than personal income. Instead, Zucman’s proposal is a “minimum tax on ultra-high net worth individuals based on their wealth”.
Zucman is specific. He proposes a minimum annual tax of 2% on fortunes exceeding US$100 million. That is the rate needed to offset the regressive features of existing tax systems.
This is not socialism; it is democracy. Zucman is not trying to send billionaires broke. He notes that on average, billionaires’ wealth grows by 6% each year. Compared to what others pay in tax, taking a third of that is entirely reasonable and still allows the billionaires to retain their status as the richest people in the world.
Better still, it is a strategy that “closes the door on tax avoidance strategies, from holding companies and trusts to shell companies”.
Despite their manifestos and pronouncements, the extraordinary fortunes of Musk, Zuckerberg and their peers demonstrate that the wealth generated by technological innovation does not automatically disperse throughout society. Instead, it has fuelled the rise of a new class of ultra-billionaires and, likely soon, trillionaires.
For now, it is probably best not to listen to Musk’s advice that there is no need to save for retirement. For all their confidence in technology’s capacity to create abundance, the tech billionaires have proven far better at amassing fortunes than sharing them.
While the tech billionaires ask us to trust in their fantastical projections of the future, Zucman offers a concrete policy proposal grounded in evidence and argument. He is one of the world’s leading economists, but his proposal is political. The real strength of his book is its democratically grounded contestation of the expansion of extreme wealth and the power it buys.
If we do not address economic inequality with fair economic policies, AI will not put us on a golden highway to Musk’s promise of universal high income and penthouses for everyone. Quite the contrary. The current trajectory is towards economic injustice, plutocratic oligarchy and political unrest.
results.summary:
Elon Musk and other tech leaders predict AI will create a post-scarcity society, while economist Gabriel Zucman argues that systemic tax reform is necessary to ensure equitable wealth distribution.

### Key Points
- Elon Musk claims AI and robotics will eliminate scarcity by 2036, potentially rendering traditional retirement savings and money irrelevant.
- Tech figures like Mark Zuckerberg and Marc Andreessen suggest that superintelligence and capitalist markets will naturally improve living standards for everyone.
- Economist Gabriel Zucman argues in his book, *We Need to Tax Billionaires*, that wealth does not distribute itself and currently remains concentrated at the top.
- Zucman reports that ultra-rich individuals often pay effective income tax rates as low as 2% by utilizing holding companies and unrealized capital gains.
- The book proposes a 2% minimum annual tax on fortunes exceeding US$100 million to curb tax avoidance and address rising global inequality.

### Why it Matters
The debate highlights a fundamental tension between techno-optimist visions of automated abundance and the reality of current economic inequality. Without concrete political mechanisms for wealth distribution, critics argue that technological progress may exacerbate plutocratic power rather than providing the universal prosperity promised by industry leaders.

results.title: How Crypto Trading Is Changing With Zero Fees and AI
results.author: Bradley Peak
results.content:
Twenty traders gathered in Bali in August for the final of Alpha Arena S03, competing live in a simulated trading environment for a share of $100,000.
The competition, backed by MEXC Ventures and held during CoinFest Asia, was won by Japan’s Arumando, followed by Murasaki Trades from the Philippines and Coin6097 from South Korea.
For MEXC CEO Vugar Usi, the competition proved that a trader can enter the market with a small amount of money, catch the right trade, and become wealthy almost overnight – an idea that has long been fundamental to crypto’s appeal.
Exposing Trading for What It Is
During Alpha Arena, Usi pointed to the difference between watching traders during an entire session and following them on social media, where successful trades can receive far more attention than the losses, uncertainty, and emotional decisions surrounding them.
At the Bali competition, traders could be observed throughout the process. Organizers even measured participants’ heart rates, allowing viewers to see how they reacted as markets moved and whether they followed their original strategy or made decisions under pressure.
“You see what kind of decisions they make. Are they panicking? Are they panic buying or panic selling? Are they good at following their instinct, or are they more practical?” Usi said.
That is part of why he believes trading has an unusually low barrier to entry compared with many professional fields. Someone can study markets independently, develop a methodology, and potentially compete against traders with formal financial training and access to far more expensive technology.
For exchanges trying to attract the next generation of users, this also changes the job. Aside from access to markets, traders also want information, analytical tools, and products that help them interpret what is happening once they arrive.
On Zero Trading Fees
Competition has become particularly fierce as major exchanges fight over trading costs.
MEXC has made zero-fee trading a big part of its strategy. Its current offering includes zero maker and taker fees across spot markets, alongside selected futures products, although eligibility and fee arrangements vary between products and campaigns. The exchange said its zero-fee initiatives saved 3.44 million users approximately 1.1 billion USDT during 2025.
Usi argues that reducing price to zero forces exchanges to compete elsewhere.
“When price is zero, it means the user is not choosing you because of just price,” he said. “That is where the competition actually starts.”
Once an exchange cannot meaningfully undercut another platform on fees, he argues, product quality, speed, available markets, trading tools, and other user benefits become more important.
Of course, the company now offers exposure to equities through several formats, including more than 300 stock and index futures, over 200 tokenized stocks, and more than 7,000 global stocks and ETFs through RealStocks, according to figures released by MEXC.
It forms part of Usi’s longer-term plan to take MEXC beyond the conventional definition of a crypto exchange.
AI Could Give Retail Traders Institutional-Level Tools
Artificial intelligence was a big part of the conversation with Usi.
His background in traditional finance influences how he thinks about trading technology. Professional firms have historically paid large sums for products such as Bloomberg Terminal because access to data, communication tools, and analytics can materially improve how traders process information.
Naturally, retail traders are put at a disadvantage.
Usi believes AI offers an opportunity to reduce that divide by taking capabilities that once required specialist software and presenting them to individual traders at a much lower cost.
In his own trading, he said he uses an AI assistant to study order books and identify where capital is concentrated, something that would be difficult for a person to continuously calculate across large amounts of market data.
“The opportunity with AI is not just to automate things,” he said, describing its potential to bring institutional-grade trading tools to retail users.
Demand appears to be coming from users themselves. Usi said a recent campaign inviting customer feedback produced more than 2,500 pages of responses, with AI emerging as the most common subject.
The important question will be how far exchanges take that assistance. Tools that summarize data, monitor markets, and surface relevant information can support traders without removing the need for judgment. Alpha Arena itself demonstrated how differently people can interpret the same market even when they have access to similar information.
Competition for Trust
Better tools and cheaper trading have limited value if users are uncomfortable holding assets on an exchange, particularly after a succession of failures and security incidents across the crypto industry.
Usi said transparency has therefore become one of his priorities since taking over as CEO of MEXC in April 2026. The appointment was something of a homecoming for BeInCrypto, where he previously served as Chief Marketing Officer before later joining Bitget and eventually MEXC.
“I don’t want the user to assume trust. I want the user to be comfortable,” he said.
MEXC publishes monthly Proof of Reserves reports audited by blockchain security company Hacken. Its August disclosure reported reserve ratios of 115% for USDT, 114% for USDC, and above 100% for other reported major assets.
The exchange has also been building its Guardian Fund. MEXC announced in May that it plans to expand the fund from $100 million toward $500 million over two years and acquired 1,000 BTC as part of its reserve arrangements.
Separately, its futures insurance fund stood at approximately 751 million USDT in its August disclosure.
Traders Want Different Things, Depending on the Market
The Bali event also gave MEXC a close look at traders across Asia-Pacific, where Usi sees different economic motivations from those common in wealthier markets.
Where disposable income is lower, a conventional investment returning several percentage points per year may make relatively little difference to someone’s finances. Some traders therefore accept considerably greater risk in search of returns large enough to have an immediate impact.
In wealthier countries, people who have already accumulated substantial assets may care more about preserving that wealth and earning steadier returns.
“In developing markets, people are more prone to make much riskier, much more leveraged trades,” Usi said, contrasting wealth generation with the greater emphasis on wealth preservation he sees in developed economies.
Usi previously worked on institutional adoption, but said one reason he joined MEXC was the company’s heavier emphasis on individual users.
“Retail comes first,” he said, noting that institutional participation is becoming a major source of crypto trading activity and exchanges are expanding products aimed at professional capital.
The Exchange of 2031?
Earlier in his career, Usi expected exchanges to gradually resemble banks. Now, he argues that the opposite has happened as banking apps have added investing, crypto, commodities, payments, and other financial products.
“In the next five years … we will be seeing these financial super apps, super platforms, gateways where we can meet all our financial needs in a single place,” he said.
MEXC is already pursuing parts of that model through crypto trading, stock products, yield products, AI-assisted trading tools, and its planned card offering.
Whether users ultimately want all of those services from one company remains an open question. What is already becoming apparent, however, is that cryptocurrency exchanges are competing across far more than the number of tokens they list.
Alpha Arena saw how traders from different countries entered the same market with the same objective, yet used different strategies and reacted differently as circumstances changed.
The exchanges serving them face a similar contest. Once access becomes cheap and trading fees approach zero, differentiation has to come from somewhere else.
results.summary:
Japan’s Arumando won the $100,000 Alpha Arena S03 trading competition in Bali, highlighting how MEXC is evolving beyond crypto to offer AI-driven tools and diverse financial products.

### Key Points
- The Alpha Arena S03 competition, held during CoinFest Asia, featured 20 traders competing in a live, simulated environment.
- MEXC reported that its zero-fee trading initiatives saved 3.44 million users approximately 1.1 billion USDT throughout 2025.
- The exchange now offers access to over 7,000 global stocks and ETFs, alongside tokenized stocks and index futures.

### Why it Matters
As trading fees approach zero across the industry, crypto exchanges are shifting their competitive focus toward product quality, advanced analytical tools, and comprehensive financial services. This transition toward "financial super apps" reflects a broader effort to capture market share by integrating traditional equities, AI-driven insights, and enhanced security measures for retail users.

Technology sector giants building the next generation of artificial intelligence require baseload power that runs continuously without interruption. That reality forces major technology firms to rapidly recognize nuclear energy as a viable solution capable of meeting these electricity demands while adhering to carbon-neutrality mandates.

results.title: Irritating Google Home bug refuses to answer your basic questions
results.author: Chethan Rao
results.content:
Irritating Google Home bug refuses to answer your basic questions
Sep 7, 2026 — 11:50 AM ET
- Some Google Home users are reportedly having trouble getting devices to answer pretty basic queries.
- Affected people note that some queries like timers and sports scores work, but asking for a recipe returns an error.
- A couple of impacted users appear to be on the older Assistant experience, with no confirmed reports coming from Gemini for Home users.
Sometimes it feels like half the time we’re talking about Google Home, we’re telling you about the latest way it’s messing up. It hasn’t been long since we reported on an issue that restricted users from adding lists to Keep, which Google has since fixed. Now, users are reporting another glitch with their Google Home devices, one that refuses to answer basic questions.
We’re seeing multiple reports on Reddit that detail the problem. One user with an unspecified smart display claims Google Home responds with an, “I’m sorry, I don’t understand that,” to a question asking whether Columbus Day is a federal holiday. The affected person points out that the voice assistant couldn’t provide a list of federal holidays, but it could define a federal holiday.
Another user with a smart speaker seems to face a similar problem, with Google Home suddenly refusing to answer simple questions on recipes and other kitchen-related topics. However, they note that other features, like setting a timer and fetching sports scores, continue to work.
More than one impacted user claims to be facing this on the older Google Assistant-based Home experience. So far we haven’t found any reports of this particular glitch from Gemini for Home users.
While there is a general sense from some of these reports that this could be Google’s way of pushing users to use Gemini, this is purely speculation until there’s evidence to suggest otherwise.
Is your Google Home device facing issues answering basic questions?
We have reached out to Google for comment on what seems like a widespread issue among Home devices, and will update this post if and when we hear anything. In the meantime, let us know if you’re facing similar problems with your Google Home smart speaker or display.
